meta.title: How to Calculate Your Monthly Mortgage Payment
meta.heading: How to Calculate Your Monthly Mortgage Payment
meta.description: Calculate mortgage principal and interest, add taxes and insurance, and compare 15- and 30-year examples. Includes the formula, Excel PMT and reproducible inputs.
meta.cardIntro: Separate loan repayment from tax, insurance and HOA costs, with three checked scenarios and a spreadsheet formula.

mortgage.intro: For a standard fixed-rate, fully amortizing mortgage, calculate the principal-and-interest installment from the loan amount, contractual interest rate and number of monthly payments. Then add property tax, homeowners insurance, applicable mortgage insurance and HOA costs to estimate a fuller housing budget. Those two answers are different: the loan formula does not automatically include the costs of owning the home.
mortgage.answer: A hypothetical $300,000 mortgage at a 6% nominal annual rate over 30 years has $1,798.65 monthly principal and interest. Entering $400 monthly property tax, $150 insurance and $100 HOA makes the initial modeled outlay $2,448.65, with no PMI in this example. These are chosen assumptions, not a current lender quote or a local tax estimate.

sections.title: Start with the loan, not the home price
paragraphs: A $375,000 purchase with a 20% down payment leaves $300,000 to finance before any financed fees. A 20% down payment is $75,000; it is not an interest charge. If you already know the financed amount, the calculator also supports entering a loan amount directly. Do not enter the purchase price as the principal unless that is actually the amount borrowed.

Use the note interest rate for the payment formula, not the APR. APR incorporates specified borrowing charges and is useful when comparing offers, but substituting it for the contractual rate changes the repayment calculation. Our example holds the rate constant, has no financed fees and assumes equal monthly periods.

sections.title: The monthly mortgage payment formula
paragraphs: Let P be principal, i the monthly interest rate as a decimal, and N the number of monthly payments. Divide a nominal annual percentage rate by 100 and by 12. Multiply a term in years by 12. Here P = 300,000, i = 0.06 / 12 = 0.005, and N = 360.

Substituting those values gives an unrounded installment of 1,798.651575458257. Displaying $1,798.65 does not mean the model rounds every internal calculation to cents. A lender’s cent-rounded installment, first-period day count and final payment can produce small differences. At 0% interest use P / N; the ordinary fraction otherwise divides by zero.

sections.title: What happens inside the first payment?
paragraphs: The first month’s interest in this equal-period example is $300,000 × 0.005 = $1,500. Subtract that from $1,798.65 to get approximately $298.65 of principal reduction. Next month, interest applies to the smaller outstanding balance. The payment remains level while the principal and interest shares change.

With no extras, the 30-year example pays approximately $347,514.57 interest across the term, before tax, insurance and other ownership costs. A shorter 15-year loan at the same illustrative rate needs $2,531.57 principal and interest monthly, but the modeled total interest falls to $155,682.69. Real 15- and 30-year quotes need not have identical rates.

sections.title: Add property tax, insurance, PMI and HOA separately
paragraphs: Convert each annual dollar cost to a monthly amount before adding it. In our worksheet, $4,800 annual tax / 12 = $400; $1,800 insurance / 12 = $150; and $1,200 HOA / 12 = $100. Their $650 sum raises the initial outlay without changing the loan’s principal-and-interest installment. HOA may be paid separately from the mortgage bill.

PMI is separate from homeowners insurance. The examples explicitly select Manual PMI and zero PMI because the illustrated down payment is 20%; they are not an estimate of every borrower’s insurance requirement. For a lower down payment, use the tool’s disclosed automatic estimate or enter an actual quote manually. Cancellation depends on the selected model and lender conditions.

Escrow is a way to collect certain bills, not an extra cost to add a second time. If a quoted total already includes escrowed tax and insurance, reconcile the components instead of adding those bills again. A fixed loan rate does not freeze taxes, insurance or escrow adjustments. Maintenance, utilities and reserves may still sit outside the payment estimate.
sections.formula: Initial housing outlay = principal and interest + annual tax/12 + annual insurance/12 + monthly PMI + annual HOA/12 + other entered costs/12

sections.title: Calculate the payment in Excel or Google Sheets
paragraphs: For this example, enter =-PMT(6%/12,30*12,300000). The minus sign converts the spreadsheet’s payment-outflow sign convention to a positive displayed payment. If your spreadsheet uses semicolons as argument separators, adjust the separators without changing the rates or periods.

PMT returns loan principal and interest, not a complete escrow or ownership budget. Add =4800/12+1800/12+1200/12 separately for the $650 monthly costs. Keep the unrounded PMT value for intermediate calculations; format the cell to two decimals for display. A zero-rate check is =300000/(30*12).

sections.title: How to compare offers without mixing assumptions
paragraphs: First hold the financed amount, term, payment frequency and cost definitions constant. Change one input, such as the rate, and compare both the payment and total interest. Then test a different down payment or term as a separate scenario. Include upfront cash and closing charges when making a broader decision; this payment example does not calculate an offer’s overall economic value.

Extra principal can shorten payoff while leaving the scheduled installment unchanged. Recasting and refinancing are different transactions. If you want to evaluate extras, open the payoff tools rather than subtracting the extra cash from interest manually. Check the loan’s prepayment terms and how the servicer applies an extra payment before acting.

mortgage.chartAlt: Three scenarios compare initial monthly principal and interest plus 650 dollars of tax, insurance and HOA: 30 years at 6 percent, 15 years at 6 percent and 30 years at zero percent.
mortgage.chartCaption: Same $300,000 financed amount and $650 monthly entered costs. These initial outlays exclude PMI, extras, maintenance and utilities. The full table supplies exact displayed values.

questions.question: How do I calculate a monthly mortgage payment with taxes and insurance?
questions.answer: Calculate principal and interest first, then add annual property tax and insurance divided by 12. Add applicable PMI, HOA and other costs once. If they already appear in an escrow-inclusive quote, do not count them twice.

questions.question: Does the mortgage payment formula include the down payment?
questions.answer: The down payment reduces the principal you borrow. It is not an extra monthly term in the amortization formula. This example borrows $300,000 after a $75,000 down payment on a $375,000 home.

questions.question: Why can a fixed-rate mortgage payment increase?
questions.answer: The contractual principal-and-interest amount may remain level while tax, insurance, mortgage insurance or an escrow adjustment changes the total bill. Review your statement’s components. Adjustable-rate, interest-only and other contracts need their own repayment assumptions.

questions.question: How much does each extra $10,000 borrowed add per month?
questions.answer: At the same 6% nominal rate and 30-year term, the fixed-payment formula is proportional to principal: an additional $10,000 adds about $59.96 monthly principal and interest. Costs or insurance triggered by a different LTV are separate.

questions.question: Is APR the rate to enter into PMT?
questions.answer: Use the loan’s contractual interest rate for its scheduled installment. APR includes specified financing charges; replacing the note rate with APR generally does not reproduce the contract payment.

questions.question: Why is my lender’s payment different from the calculator?
questions.answer: Check principal, rate, term, financed charges, PMI, taxes, insurance, escrow adjustments and rounding. Irregular first periods, lender conventions and a different loan product can also change the result. A model is not a binding Loan Estimate.

limitations: The three cases assume monthly, fixed-rate, fully amortizing loans, no extra repayments and no financed fees. Costs are entered estimates and held constant.
No qualification, local tax determination, tax deduction, ARM reset or insurance quote is inferred. A zero-rate case is an arithmetic boundary check, not an available offer.

meta.title: How Compound Interest Works With Monthly Contributions
meta.heading: How Compound Interest Works With Monthly Contributions
meta.description: Work through compound growth with monthly deposits, beginning versus end timing, nominal rate versus APY, Excel formulas and four checked scenarios.
meta.cardIntro: Four matched scenarios separate money you contribute from earnings and show the effect of deposit timing.

compound.intro: Compound growth with monthly contributions has two sources: your starting balance grows, and each new deposit grows for the months it remains invested. Deposits made later have less time to earn a return. A useful worksheet therefore separates contributions from earnings and states whether deposits arrive at the beginning or end of each month.
compound.answer: With $10,000 initially, $200 at every month end, ten years and a constant 5% nominal annual rate compounded monthly, the modeled ending balance is $47,526.55. You supply $34,000; the remaining $13,526.55 is modeled earnings before tax and fees. These assumed rates are not current bank offers or forecasts.

sections.title: State the rate, contribution schedule and time horizon
paragraphs: Our four cases use 120 months, $10,000 starting money and $200 each month. Annual deposits, tax and inflation inputs are all zero. Selecting monthly compounding makes a 5% nominal annual rate equal to 0.05 / 12 per month. That convention is essential to reproducing the figures.

A nominal annual rate and APY are not interchangeable. If your quoted yield is a 5% effective APY, the equivalent monthly growth factor is 1.05^(1/12), not 1 + 0.05/12. The tool’s rate-conversion mode can translate an effective annual rate, entered as an annual-compounding rate, into a monthly-compounding nominal rate. Do not add a second compounding benefit to an APY.

sections.title: The formula for monthly deposits at month end
paragraphs: Let P be starting principal, C the monthly deposit, i the monthly rate and N the number of months. The first term compounds the initial balance. The second is the future value of the deposit series. It assumes one deposit at the end of every month and no missed deposits or withdrawals.

For the worked example, i = 0.05/12, N = 120, P = 10,000 and C = 200. Applying the formula gives $47,526.55. If i is zero, use P + C × N: $10,000 + $200 × 120 = $34,000. This zero-rate check helps detect accidentally counting your own deposits as investment profit.

sections.title: Separate deposits from investment earnings
paragraphs: Total contributions in every case are $10,000 + $24,000 = $34,000. At 5% with month-end deposits, the model adds $13,526.55 of net earnings before any tax input. Reporting the full $47,526.55 as profit would overstate what the investment earned.

For comparison, the starting $10,000 alone grows to about $16,470.09 at the same rate and horizon. The remaining balance comes from the monthly deposits and their earnings. Regular saving is doing substantial work here; the result is not evidence that compounding makes contributions unnecessary.

sections.title: Month-start deposits earn one extra monthly period
paragraphs: A beginning-of-month contribution arrives before that month’s growth. Multiply only the deposit-series term by (1 + i). The initial principal is already invested at time zero, so do not multiply the entire ending balance by an extra month.

At 5%, switching the same 120 deposits to month start raises the ending balance to $47,655.95, a $129.40 difference after rounding. That is a timing effect, not a higher assumed return. A real payroll or brokerage schedule can have more varied dates; this worksheet uses regular monthly intervals.
sections.formula: Beginning-of-month deposit value = C × [(1 + i)^N − 1] / i × (1 + i)

sections.title: Use FV in a spreadsheet and verify the signs
paragraphs: For month-end deposits, enter =FV(5%/12,10*12,-200,-10000,0). Negative contributions denote cash you put into the account; the positive answer is the future balance received. Change the final argument to 1 for deposits at the beginning of each month.

To check the no-deposit result, use =FV(5%/12,120,0,-10000,0). To check zero growth without dividing by zero, use =10000+200*120. Currency formatting is a display choice: do not round every intermediate growth step simply to make the cell show cents.

sections.title: Test uncertainty without presenting a forecast
paragraphs: Keeping the contributions fixed but assuming 8% nominal growth produces $58,785.61 after ten years, compared with $47,526.55 at 5%. The $11,259.06 difference shows sensitivity to the chosen rate. It is not evidence that a particular portfolio will earn either return or that the higher-return case is equally attainable.

The actual calculator can also apply annual deposits, contribution increases in supported tools, tax on positive interest and inflation. Those settings are outside these four matched cases. Its monthly-equivalent growth convention does not reproduce every bank’s daily balance, deposit processing or interest-crediting method.

The tax input applies the model’s simplified charge to positive accrued interest at year end; it is not a capital-gains or retirement-account tax engine. Inflation-adjusted balances measure purchasing power rather than extra nominal earnings. Investment fees, losses and irregular withdrawals need explicit treatment instead of being hidden in an optimistic rate.

compound.chartAlt: Four 10-year scenarios have identical 34,000 dollar total contributions but different modeled earnings at zero, five and eight percent, including month-start and month-end deposits.
compound.chartCaption: Constant nominal rates with monthly compounding; $10,000 initially and 120 deposits of $200. No annual deposits, tax, inflation or fees. Both principal and deposits are included in contributions.

questions.question: How do I calculate compound interest with monthly contributions?
questions.answer: Compound the starting amount and add the future value of the monthly deposit series. Use one consistent monthly rate, a whole-month count and the correct deposit timing. Subtract total contributions from the final balance to isolate earnings.

questions.question: Can I use an annual APY divided by 12?
questions.answer: That is an approximation, not the exact monthly equivalent. For APY use i = (1 + APY)^(1/12) − 1, with APY in decimal form. Divide by 12 when the stated rate is nominal with monthly compounding.

questions.question: Does depositing at the beginning of the month make a difference?
questions.answer: Yes, at a positive rate the deposit series earns one more month of growth per deposit. In the matched 5% case it adds $129.40 to the ten-year ending balance. At zero growth the timing does not change the result.

questions.question: Are monthly contributions included in compound interest?
questions.answer: They are included in the ending balance, but are your money rather than earned interest. Here $34,000 of the final balance is contributed money. Read the earnings field separately.

questions.question: Can I compare monthly deposits with one annual deposit?
questions.answer: Yes, but match the total annual contribution and specify the annual deposit date. Twelve month-end deposits are not economically identical to one deposit at the beginning or end of the year. Keep the rate convention consistent.

questions.question: Does daily compounding always produce a larger balance?
questions.answer: At the same positive nominal annual rate, more frequent compounding increases effective yield. At the same APY the effective annual yield is already matched. Fees, changing rates and cash-flow timing may matter more than that isolated frequency effect.

limitations: All four examples use constant monthly rates and nominal USD, with no tax, fees, inflation, withdrawals or skipped deposits. They are model scenarios, not historical investment results.
The selector converts the stated compounding frequency to a monthly equivalent for this projection. Exact day-count and bank interest-crediting conventions are not simulated.

meta.title: Annualized Return vs. Total Return: How to Calculate and Compare
meta.heading: Annualized Return vs. Total Return: How to Calculate and Compare
meta.description: Compare cumulative and annualized returns with checked holding-period and loss examples. Includes formulas, Excel and limits when deposits or withdrawals occur.
meta.cardIntro: The same 50% cumulative gain becomes a different annualized return over one, three or five years.

annualized.intro: Total return measures the gain or loss across the entire holding period. Annualized return expresses a compatible result as a constant compounded yearly rate. Neither figure describes the path your investment actually took, and the simple endpoint formula works only when the beginning and ending amounts represent the same invested capital without intervening external cash flows.
annualized.answer: A single $10,000 investment ending at $15,000 has a 50% cumulative return. Held for three years, its compound annualized return is 14.4714%; held for five years, it is 8.4472%. Dividing 50% by the number of years would give a simple average of the total gain, not the compound annual rate.

sections.title: What total return and annualized return each answer
paragraphs: A cumulative return asks how much value changed relative to the original investment over the stated period. A compound annualized return asks what constant yearly growth rate would connect those endpoints. A 50% gain over one year and the same gain over five years are not the same rate of growth per year.

Terminology varies across statements. In these examples, cumulative return is the ROI of one initial outlay and one terminal value, with no intervening payouts or contributions. If a statement uses total return to include reinvested distributions, make sure the terminal value uses the same convention. A price-only change omits dividends; a net-of-fee return differs from gross performance.

sections.title: Calculate the cumulative gain and the compound yearly rate
paragraphs: Let B be the positive beginning value, E the nonnegative ending value, and T the holding period in years. Cumulative return is E / B − 1. Compound annualized return is (E / B)^(1 / T) − 1. Multiply each decimal result by 100 to display a percentage. A meaningful annualization needs a positive holding period.

For $10,000 becoming $15,000 over three years: E / B = 1.5, so 1.5^(1/3) − 1 = approximately 0.14471424. This is 14.4714% annually. Recompounding (1.14471424)^3 approximately reproduces 1.5; ordinary 50% / 3 = 16.6667% does not.

This endpoint calculation is often called CAGR. Its constant rate is a mathematical equivalent, not a claim that each year earned the same amount. Volatility, drawdowns, liquidity and the risk taken are absent from the ratio.
sections.formula: Cumulative return = (E / B − 1) × 100%; annualized return = [(E / B)^(1 / T) − 1] × 100%

sections.title: Keep the investment unchanged while testing the holding period
paragraphs: Our first three cases use the same $10,000 starting cost and $15,000 terminal amount. Only the holding period changes: one, three or five years. Cumulative ROI remains 50% while the annualized rate falls from 50% to 14.4714% and then 8.4472%. The chart compares the percentages; the table includes reproducible calculator inputs.

This is a controlled arithmetic comparison, not a choice between actual investments. Different holding periods can involve different risks and availability. An annualized rate alone does not say whether an asset was accessible, diversified or suitable for your cash needs.

sections.title: Annualization also applies to a loss
paragraphs: If $10,000 becomes $8,000 over two years with no cash flows, cumulative return is −20% and compound annualized return is approximately −10.5573%. Two years of a constant −10% would instead leave $8,100. That is why simply dividing a cumulative loss by years gives the wrong compound equivalent.

At a zero terminal value, the mathematical compound rate is −100% for a positive holding period; it does not reveal when the loss occurred. Negative terminal equity, leverage, debt and cash-flow liabilities require a model that represents those obligations. Do not force them into a standard positive-capital CAGR example.

sections.title: When deposits or withdrawals make the shortcut misleading
paragraphs: Suppose an account starts with $10,000, receives a $5,000 deposit at the very end of year three and then displays $15,000. With zero market gains, the account has still grown in dollars. Calling that a 50% investment return would misclassify the new deposit as profit. Our ROI tool does not have an intermediate-cash-flow schedule; its endpoint rate is not appropriate for that account history.

For regularly spaced signed cash flows, an IRR calculation can estimate a money-weighted rate if a meaningful solution exists. Irregular dated flows need their actual dates, for example a spreadsheet XIRR calculation. A time-weighted return instead chains subperiod performance while separating external flows. These measures answer different questions; do not label them interchangeable.

Likewise, adding every dividend to the terminal amount ignores when the dividends arrived if you then annualize. Our no-distribution cases avoid that timing problem. For an income investment, state whether distributions were reinvested, retained as cash or spent and choose a method consistent with that history.

sections.title: Excel formulas and a useful reverse check
paragraphs: For the three-year example, =15000/10000-1 returns 0.5, which a percentage-formatted cell displays as 50%. =(15000/10000)^(1/3)-1 returns about 14.4714% when formatted as a percentage. Do not multiply by 100 and also apply percentage formatting, or the displayed result will be 100 times too large.

Check your calculation by reversing it: =10000*(1+annualized_rate)^3 should reproduce $15,000, using the unrounded decimal annualized rate. For actual dates, the tool’s Use Dates mode uses actual elapsed days divided by 365 as its year convention. A spreadsheet YEARFRAC basis may produce a slightly different answer, so document the convention instead of calling either a universal standard.

sections.title: Annualized return is different from an arithmetic average
paragraphs: Consider +20% in year one and −20% in year two. The arithmetic average is 0%, but $10,000 becomes $9,600 because 1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96. The two-year geometric annual rate is sqrt(0.96) − 1, approximately −2.0204%. Equal positive and negative percentages do not cancel when they compound.

Use the Average Return Calculator to distinguish the arithmetic mean of periodic percentages from their compounded geometric mean. Use ROI for compatible beginning and terminal amounts, and IRR for supported periodic cash flows. None of these calculations forecasts next year’s performance or measures every dimension of investment risk.

annualized.chartAlt: For a 50 percent cumulative gain, annualized return is 50 percent over one year, 14.4714 percent over three years and 8.4472 percent over five years.
annualized.chartCaption: One initial $10,000 investment and a $15,000 terminal value with no intermediate flows. The loss case appears in the table, not in this matched-gain chart.

questions.question: Is annualized return the same as total return?
questions.answer: No. Total or cumulative return describes the whole stated period. Annualized return converts a compatible multi-year result into an equivalent compound yearly rate. They coincide for a one-year endpoint example with the same cash-flow definition.

questions.question: How do I convert cumulative return to annualized return?
questions.answer: Use (1 + cumulative_decimal)^(1 / years) − 1. For 50% cumulative over three years, use 1.5^(1/3) − 1, approximately 14.4714%. This assumes a compatible return definition and no omitted external cash flows.

questions.question: Can I divide my total gain by the number of years?
questions.answer: That produces a simple average of the total gain rather than a compound annual equivalent. Use the power formula if you want a yearly rate that compounds back to the same terminal amount.

questions.question: Is annualized return the same as an average annual return?
questions.answer: Not necessarily. Average may refer to an arithmetic mean of yearly percentages, while compound annualized return is geometric. State the definition and check whether cash flows and distributions were treated consistently.

questions.question: Can I annualize a return earned in less than one year?
questions.answer: Mathematically yes, using the fraction of a year, but a short-period result extrapolated to a year can be misleading. It does not show that the return can be repeated or that the same risk and liquidity conditions will persist.

questions.question: Where do fees, taxes and dividends belong?
questions.answer: Use consistent beginning and terminal values and disclose gross versus net treatment. Intermediate distributions, taxes paid outside the account and extra deposits may require a cash-flow model. The ROI calculator does not calculate your personal tax liability.

limitations: The four displayed endpoint cases have no dividends, interim deposits, withdrawals, fees or taxes. Their percentages are before inflation. The arithmetic-average illustration is separate from those four cases.
Annualization is descriptive, not a forecast, risk score or guarantee. Dated calculations depend on the specified day-count convention.

meta.title: What Is House Hacking? Costs, Rent Offsets & Examples
meta.heading: What Is House Hacking? Costs, Rent Offsets & Examples
meta.description: Understand house hacking with rooms or rental units, upfront cash and net housing costs. Compare four rent-loss cases with checked inputs and a calculator.
meta.cardIntro: Four rent-loss scenarios show when tenant income lowers a housing budget and when the same property costs more than renting.

house.intro: House hacking means living in part of a property while renting other rooms or units to tenants. Rent can offset some of your housing costs, but the mortgage installment is only one expense. A useful calculation separates the initial cash needed to buy from the recurring cost of living there, and includes the possibility that tenant income falls short.
house.answer: In our hypothetical shared-home example, two rooms each rent for $750 monthly. With a 5% rent-loss allowance, the modeled owner housing cost is $1,593.56 a month after tenant rent, versus an entered $1,800 alternative renting budget. That $206.44 monthly budget difference is not investment profit: the purchase also requires $98,000 upfront, and taxes, sale proceeds and opportunity cost are not compared.

sections.title: Renting rooms versus renting a separate unit
paragraphs: Both arrangements combine your own home with rented space. In a shared home, tenants rent specified rooms while you remain in the property. In a multi-unit arrangement, you occupy one unit and rent others. Separate entrances, utility arrangements, maintenance responsibilities and privacy can change the practical trade-offs even when the arithmetic looks similar.

Our calculator lets you describe either arrangement and enter each tenant space. Your own room or unit is excluded from rent income. The arrangement selector does not establish zoning compliance, a tenancy classification or mortgage eligibility. A legal rental unit and an advertised bedroom are not automatically interchangeable.

sections.title: Build the initial cash requirement before the monthly budget
paragraphs: The example purchases a $400,000 property using a $320,000 loan. Cash toward the price is $80,000. Add $8,000 cash-paid closing costs and loan fees, $5,000 initial repairs and $5,000 initial reserve cash to reach $98,000 required at acquisition. Those are chosen inputs, not a claim about a minimum down payment or lender reserve requirement.

Borrowing is not tenant income. Keep refundable tenant deposits separate as well: cash held for a tenant is not freely available recurring revenue. Count an initial repair once in acquisition cash; do not also call the same payment a new recurring monthly maintenance bill. A future maintenance allowance represents a different period and purpose.
sections.formula: Initial cash = purchase price − purchase loan + cash-paid closing costs + initial repairs + initial reserve

sections.title: Calculate the whole-property cash cost, then offset tenant rent
paragraphs: At an illustrative 6% nominal annual loan rate over 30 years, monthly principal and interest on $320,000 is $1,918.56. Our entered monthly costs add $400 property tax, $150 property insurance, $200 owner-paid utilities, $200 routine maintenance and $150 capital replacement reserve. Mortgage insurance, HOA, management and other costs are explicitly zero in these cases. Total cost before rent is $3,018.56 monthly.

Two tenant rooms at $750 produce $1,500 scheduled monthly rent. Apply a 5% vacancy and collection-loss allowance to get $1,425 effective rent. Subtract that from $3,018.56 to get $1,593.56 of net housing cash cost. The owner’s own space contributes no imaginary rent, and no other income is entered.

Principal repayment is included in the cash you must pay even though it reduces debt and can build equity. It is not spendable income to add back to this budget. Also avoid entering an escrow-inclusive loan bill and then adding its taxes and insurance again. The model calculates principal and interest separately from those ownership costs.
sections.formula: Net monthly housing cash cost = mortgage P&I + entered owner costs + capital reserve − rent after losses − other net housing income

sections.title: Test what happens when tenant income is interrupted
paragraphs: Our four cases hold the loan, rooms, upfront cash and all owner costs fixed. Only the rent-loss allowance changes from 0% to 5%, 20% and 100%. At zero loss, the net housing cost is $1,518.56. At 20%, it rises to $1,818.56, slightly above the $1,800 renting alternative. With no tenant rent collected it is $3,018.56.

A percentage allowance is an expected monthly provision; it does not identify which actual month a tenant leaves or a repair occurs. The 100% case is a stress check for paying the bills without rent, not a forecast of long-run vacancy. A reserve sufficient for one month may not cover a prolonged interruption or a large replacement.

For this example, recurring costs exceed rent even at full collection, so it does not model living for free. A different input set can show a negative net housing cost, but that is only a modeled cash surplus before owner income tax, not a guarantee of a profitable or low-risk property.

sections.title: Compare like-for-like living budgets, not just rent and mortgage
paragraphs: The alternative renting budget should include comparable utilities, renters insurance and other housing costs you would otherwise pay. Here it is a manually entered all-in $1,800 per month. Subtract the net house-hacking cash cost to obtain a recurring budget difference. A positive number means the modeled housing budget is lower; a negative one means it is higher.

This comparison does not price the $98,000 upfront commitment, future sale costs, appreciation, tax treatment or the return that cash could earn elsewhere. It also does not put a dollar value on privacy, time as a landlord or the flexibility to move. A monthly budget improvement is useful, but it is not a full buy-versus-rent wealth comparison.

If you move out and rent the entire property later, your owner-occupancy budget is no longer the same scenario. Update insurance, management, maintenance and financing assumptions in the rental-property tools. Do not simply add rent for your former room while assuming every other cost stays appropriate.

sections.title: Check financing, local permission and tax treatment separately
paragraphs: Before using a listing’s advertised rent, verify that the relevant spaces can be rented as intended and check local requirements, HOA restrictions, lease obligations and the insurance policy. These depend on the property and location; the calculator does not issue a legal or lender approval. An owner-occupied loan may also come with occupancy conditions.

Renting part of a home can involve allocating expenses between personal and rental use. IRS Publication 527 discusses rental property and mixed-use situations, but this worksheet does not compute deductible shares, depreciation or your tax return. Its housing cost is a cash-budget figure before owner income tax.

Use the result as a checklist for missing inputs and an invitation to test weaker rents or higher costs. A promising default result is not evidence that a particular property, tenant or financing arrangement will work. Review the actual costs and cash available before committing to a purchase.

house.chartAlt: Net monthly housing cash cost rises from 1518.56 dollars at zero rent loss to 3018.56 dollars at complete rent loss; the alternative renting budget is 1800 dollars.
house.chartCaption: Same $400,000 property, $320,000 loan at 6% for 30 years and $1,100 monthly non-P&I costs, including a capital reserve. Only tenant rent loss changes. A higher bar means more owner cash is needed.

questions.question: What is house hacking in real estate?
questions.answer: It is living in part of a property while renting other rooms or units. Tenant rent can offset housing costs, but upfront cash, ongoing expenses, landlord duties and the risk of lost rent remain.

questions.question: Can I house hack a single-family home?
questions.answer: Renting rooms can be a house-hacking arrangement, but whether a specific setup is permitted depends on local rules, contracts and insurance. The room example illustrates a budget and does not establish legal permission or loan eligibility.

questions.question: How much money do I need to house hack?
questions.answer: Add the cash purchase contribution, closing and loan fees, initial repairs and initial reserve. This example needs $98,000; that amount is an assumption, not a universal requirement. Keep reserves for ongoing living costs and interruptions in the plan.

questions.question: Is house hacking worth it if rent does not cover the mortgage?
questions.answer: That question needs a whole-budget and risk comparison. Rent can reduce your housing cost without paying every bill, but taxes, maintenance, reserves and the opportunity cost of upfront cash still matter. The model does not issue a recommendation.

questions.question: Does tenant rent count as profit?
questions.answer: Gross rent is revenue, not profit. In an owner-occupied budget it offsets costs. The displayed difference versus renting also includes your own housing consumption, so it is not a rental investment return.

questions.question: Does the calculator include FHA or VA qualification?
questions.answer: No. The guide uses an entered loan amount and a standard fixed-rate payment. Down-payment eligibility, rental-income underwriting, occupancy conditions and mortgage-insurance rules require a separate review.

limitations: This is an immediately stabilized monthly budget, not a multi-year wealth forecast. The rate, rents and costs are hypothetical and constant in each case.
No legal permission, lender approval, income-tax allocation, sale, depreciation, appreciation or return on the upfront cash is calculated.

meta.title: How to Calculate Cash-on-Cash Return: Costs & Examples
meta.heading: How to Calculate Cash-on-Cash Return: Costs & Examples
meta.description: Calculate rental cash-on-cash return using cash invested, operating costs, debt service and reserves. Five checked scenarios include losses and a cash purchase.
meta.cardIntro: Build the numerator and denominator explicitly, then test loan cost, reserves and lower rent without hiding negative cash flow.

cash.intro: Cash-on-cash return compares annual cash flow with the cash you invested. For a financed rental, deduct operating expenses and cash debt payments before dividing by a clearly stated cash basis. This guide also deducts an ongoing capital replacement reserve from the headline yield. It is a one-year cash measure, not total property return, appreciation or a compound annual growth rate.
cash.answer: Our hypothetical $300,000 rental uses a $200,000 loan and $120,000 total initial cash including closing costs, repairs and reserves. After the entered rent loss, operating costs, first-year principal and interest and capital allowance, annual cash flow is $2,710.79. Dividing by $120,000 gives 2.2590% cash-on-cash return before owner income tax.

sections.title: Write the cash-on-cash formula with a stated period
paragraphs: Use cash flow for a defined period, normally a full year, and a cash-investment amount consistent with the question. A $6,000 annual cash flow on $60,000 invested is a 10% annual cash yield. If you enter a recurring monthly cash flow in simple mode, the tool multiplies it by 12; it does not convert an irregular distribution into a growth rate.

The numerator in our rental worksheet is before owner income tax and after the stated capital allowance. Other sources may quote a yield before reserves or use a different cash basis. A percentage is comparable only after reconciling those definitions. The tool separately shows a before-reserve figure to make the deduction visible.
sections.formula: Cash-on-cash return (%) = annual cash flow after stated costs and financing / positive cash invested × 100

sections.title: Build the denominator from actual cash committed
paragraphs: For the base case, a $300,000 price minus a $200,000 purchase loan leaves $100,000 cash toward the price. Add $5,000 cash-paid closing costs and loan fees, $10,000 initial cash repairs and $5,000 initial reserve to get $120,000 invested. The denominator is not the $300,000 property value and not the $200,000 borrowed.

Keep the meaning of reserve cash explicit. Initial reserve is cash set aside at acquisition and included in our investment basis. The ongoing monthly replacement allowance is a deduction from period cash flow. These represent different quantities; do not duplicate one repair or one reserve contribution in several lines.

Using current equity instead of initial cash would ask a different question. After refinancing, reconcile cash returned, new fees and debt separately rather than silently replacing the denominator with an attractive smaller number. A zero or negative cash basis has no meaningful positive cash-on-cash percentage in this tool.

sections.title: Calculate NOI, then deduct financing and the capital provision
paragraphs: Scheduled rent is $2,500 per month. A 5% vacancy and collection-loss allowance reduces effective rent to $2,375. With no other net income and $850 monthly operating expenses, annual NOI is ($2,375 − $850) × 12 = $18,300. Operating costs should already include the applicable property tax, insurance, routine maintenance, management, HOA and owner-paid utilities.

The $200,000 mortgage at 6% nominal interest over 30 years requires about $1,199.10 monthly principal and interest. Its first 12 unrounded scheduled payments total $14,389.21. Deduct that and a $1,200 annual capital replacement allowance from $18,300 to get $2,710.79 cash flow. No additional financing payments are entered.

NOI excludes loan payments and the separate capital provision in this worksheet. Cash-on-cash includes their cash effect. Using NOI as the numerator would overstate cash available to this owner. Initial repairs are already in acquisition cash and are not deducted again as if they occurred every year.
sections.formula: Annual cash flow = effective operating income − operating expenses − actual first-year P&I − other financing payments − capital allowance

sections.title: Why principal repayment is not added back to cash income
paragraphs: A mortgage installment pays both interest and principal. Principal reduces the outstanding debt and may increase equity, but the cash has still left the owner’s account. It cannot simultaneously be treated as spendable annual income. Equity growth belongs in a broader return analysis rather than this cash-yield numerator.

Similarly, appreciation is not rental cash received. A sale or refinance can generate cash but also involves fees, debt repayment and timing that a one-year stabilized operating yield does not describe. Use a holding-period or refinance model for those events rather than combining a one-time receipt with recurring rent.

sections.title: Five cases show how a positive yield can become a loss
paragraphs: The base case returns 2.2590%. Paying cash for the same property requires $320,000 including the same acquisition extras, produces $17,100 annual cash flow after reserve and yields 5.3438%. In this selected example, debt does not increase the cash yield. That result is conditional, not a general argument for or against borrowing.

Changing only the base loan rate from 6% to 8% turns annual cash flow into a $510.35 loss and the yield into −0.4253%. Raising only the monthly reserve from $100 to $300 leaves $310.79 annual cash flow, or 0.2590%. Reducing only the scheduled rent to $2,250 leaves a $139.21 annual loss, or −0.1160%.

Every non-base row makes one change from the base; they are separate scenarios, not a sequence of cumulative changes. The rent scenario keeps dollar operating expenses fixed. If management charges or other costs actually scale with rent, update those inputs separately. Neither the rates nor the rent figures are current market quotes.

sections.title: Cash yield and cap rate are different measurements
paragraphs: Cap rate uses NOI relative to the property price or a stated value basis. Cash-on-cash uses cash flow after financing relative to cash invested. In the base case, the price-based cap rate is $18,300 / $300,000 = 6.1%, while the after-reserve cash yield is 2.2590%. They can differ without either calculation being an error.

The cash-purchase and financed cases share the same NOI and purchase price; changing only financing leaves that cap rate unchanged. Changing rent can change NOI and therefore the cap rate. For a direct comparison of these measures, use the existing cap-rate-versus-cash-on-cash glossary analysis linked below rather than expecting this one-year cash guide to measure total return.

sections.title: Use the yield with liquidity and model limits
paragraphs: There is no universal good cash-on-cash return independent of cost definitions, risk, location, reserves and alternative uses for cash. A high percentage can reflect a small denominator or omitted expenses. Inspect both dollar cash flow and cash invested before comparing percentages.

Our worksheet models the first 12 months of immediate stabilized operation. It uses actual scheduled principal and interest in that modeled year; if a supported loan ends early, it does not charge 12 full payments after payoff. It does not simulate leasing delays, a renovation period, changing rents, future sales or owner tax. These limitations matter when applying a stable annual yield to an unsettled acquisition.

cash.chartAlt: Five same-property scenarios have cash-on-cash yields of 2.2590, 5.3438, minus 0.4253, 0.2590 and minus 0.1160 percent, showing adverse loan and rent cases.
cash.chartCaption: Each case makes one change from the base $300,000 purchase. Cash flow is before owner income tax and after the stated reserve. Percentages are not risk-adjusted forecasts.

questions.question: How do I calculate cash-on-cash return?
questions.answer: Divide a clearly defined annual cash-flow total by positive cash invested and multiply by 100. For a rental, state how operating expenses, debt service and capital reserves enter the numerator, and what upfront costs enter the denominator.

questions.question: Is cash-on-cash return calculated before or after the mortgage?
questions.answer: For the financed cash yield used here, deduct actual principal and interest payments and other stated financing cash costs first. A return calculated from NOI before financing is not the same cash-on-cash numerator.

questions.question: Do I include closing costs and initial repairs?
questions.answer: They are included when you fund them from cash under this acquisition basis. Add each once, alongside the cash toward the price and the initial reserve. Different cash-basis conventions must be disclosed before comparing yields.

questions.question: Can cash-on-cash return be negative?
questions.answer: Yes. Negative annual cash flow divided by positive cash invested gives a negative yield. The 8% loan and lower-rent examples retain that result rather than hiding the loss.

questions.question: Is cash-on-cash return the same as ROI or IRR?
questions.answer: No. This is a period cash yield. Total ROI can include other gains and costs; IRR considers supported cash-flow timing across a holding period. A one-year yield does not capture the sale, appreciation or changing equity.

questions.question: What if I recovered all my cash through a refinance?
questions.answer: Do not report an infinite or automatically favorable cash yield. Reconcile the financing event and remaining cash basis. The tool marks a zero or negative basis as not applicable for a percentage; BRRRR is the more relevant refinance worksheet.

limitations: Five cases describe the first year of an immediately stabilized property with constant monthly operating inputs and fixed-rate amortization. They are not observed deals or return forecasts.
The headline deducts a separate capital allowance and uses initial cash including reserve; no owner income tax, appreciation, sale or refinance is calculated.

meta.title: How to Calculate Landed Cost: Shipment & Per-Unit Examples
meta.heading: How to Calculate Landed Cost: Shipment & Per-Unit Examples
meta.description: Build landed cost from a shipment invoice, freight and entered import charges. Four checked cases show per-unit costs, sensitivity and how to avoid double counting.
meta.cardIntro: Reconcile itemized and bundled quotes for 500 identical units, then test freight and entered duty amounts before using cost in pricing.

landed.intro: Landed cost brings a product invoice and the additional costs of getting that shipment to its intended destination into one economic cost estimate. Start with the invoice and add only charges not already included. Then allocate the reconciled total across the units. The result can support pricing, but it is not automatically a customs valuation, tax determination or complete cost of running the business.
landed.answer: For an illustrative 500-unit shipment, a $5,000 goods invoice plus $1,800 of separately entered transport, insurance and import-related charges gives $6,800 total landed cost, or $13.60 per unit. The $10 invoice price per unit alone misses $3.60 of additional acquisition cost. All duty and tax amounts in these examples are manual assumptions, not current tariff rates.

sections.title: Define what shipment and destination the quote covers
paragraphs: Write down the product, quantity, currency and destination before adding fees. Our examples use one homogeneous product, 500 identical units and USD throughout. A total shipment amount belongs in a shipment field; entering a per-unit invoice price there would understate the total by a factor of quantity.

Reconcile who is paying each charge under the actual contract and what the invoice already includes. A quote that includes international freight should not receive that same freight as an extra cost. This worksheet does not interpret Incoterms, assign contractual obligations or convert currencies. Convert and document foreign-currency amounts consistently before using its USD fields.

sections.title: Add the applicable charges once, then divide by quantity
paragraphs: The base worksheet enters $5,000 goods, $800 international freight, $50 shipment insurance, $400 duties, $150 nonrecoverable import taxes, $100 brokerage, $75 port or handling, $200 inland transport and $25 other acquisition expenses. The additional charges sum to $1,800. Total economic acquisition cost is therefore $6,800.

Dividing by 500 units gives $13.60 each. Keep the shipment total until allocation is complete, rather than rounding every component per unit first. The additional $1,800 equals a 36% uplift over the $5,000 goods invoice. That uplift is a cost comparison, not a sales margin or a statutory duty rate.
sections.formula: Total landed cost = entered invoice + additional freight + insurance + duties + nonrecoverable taxes + brokerage + handling + inland transport + other acquisition charges; unit cost = total / units

sections.title: An itemized quote and a bundled quote can have the same total
paragraphs: Suppose a checked invoice bundles exactly the same $6,800 economic total, and no further charges remain payable within the defined destination boundary. Entering $6,800 as the invoice amount and zero additional charges gives the same $13.60 per unit. The final case demonstrates that reconciliation, not a universal rule about every bundled shipping term.

If you instead enter the bundled $6,800 invoice and add the already included $1,800 again, the mistaken total becomes $8,600, or $17.20 per unit. That would overstate this specific acquisition cost by $3.60 per unit. The itemized and bundled views must describe the same included services for the comparison to be valid.

In the bundled case, the field labeled goods invoice contains bundled charges as well as the underlying goods price. Its displayed invoice cost per unit is therefore not a separately established manufacturing cost. Do not infer customs value, a duty base or accounting classification from how the economic total was entered.

sections.title: Test freight and entered duty amounts without inventing tariff rates
paragraphs: In one scenario, only freight rises from $800 to $1,600. Total cost becomes $7,600, or $15.20 per unit. In another, freight returns to the base amount and the manually entered duties rise from $400 to $1,200. That also produces $7,600 and $15.20 per unit. These are separate scenarios, not a combined increase.

An additional $800 shipment charge spread over 500 identical units adds $1.60 each. If both increases applied at once, the inputs would need to show both; the separate cases do not imply a joint forecast. Quantity changes also need a new quote because freight, insurance and other charges may not stay fixed.

The duty field accepts a dollar amount. The tool does not determine the product classification, origin, customs valuation, tariff rate, exemption, entry date or eligibility for a trade program. A broker or the relevant official source must support those inputs for a real shipment. A 36% overall cost uplift does not mean the duty rate is 36%.

sections.title: Use a suitable allocation method for mixed products
paragraphs: Equal per-unit allocation is appropriate only for the homogeneous-unit assumption used here. If a shipment contains small low-value items and large high-value items, spreading all costs evenly per item may distort product economics. Freight may follow weight or volume, while another charge may follow value or a product-specific basis.

The calculator does not choose or implement that mixed-product allocation. Split the analysis using a documented method and reconcile the allocated amounts back to the shipment total. Changing the denominator to sellable units after damage or breakage is also a separate decision: the current input counts the shipment units you enter, not an automatic loss estimate.

sections.title: Separate economic cost from cash needed at clearance
paragraphs: Our economic-cost model excludes taxes that are actually recoverable by the business. A recoverable amount can still require cash before recovery, so the cash needed to receive a shipment can exceed the cost carried in this worksheet. Whether a particular tax is recoverable is outside the calculation and depends on the relevant facts and rules.

The $150 tax input in the base example is explicitly assumed nonrecoverable. It is not a statement that a US shipment owes VAT or that a universal import tax applies. Similarly, brokerage and handling are chosen estimates; no current official fee schedule is embedded in the guide.

sections.title: Move from landed cost to pricing without confusing margin and markup
paragraphs: At a $20 selling price and the base $13.60 acquisition cost, the difference is $6.40 per unit before other costs. Dividing $6.40 by the $20 selling price gives a 32% margin on this limited cost basis. It is not net profit: marketplace fees, payment processing, outbound fulfillment, advertising, returns, storage and overhead may still reduce it.

A 30% markup on $13.60 instead sets price at $17.68. The resulting margin is approximately 23.08%, because markup divides by cost while margin divides by selling price. Use the linked Margin and Markup tools for those distinct calculations. A target margin is only as useful as the cost boundary behind it.

Before setting a selling price, replace sample estimates with reconciled quotes, record the currency conversion and identify costs intentionally excluded. Revisit the worksheet when the invoice, shipping route, quantity or applicable charges change. A precise-looking unit cost does not make the underlying estimates certain.

landed.chartAlt: An itemized and a reconciled bundled quote each total 6800 dollars for 500 units; separate higher-freight and higher-duty cases each total 7600 dollars.
landed.chartCaption: 500 homogeneous units in every case, all USD. The bundled invoice already includes the same economic charges as the itemized base; no duty or tax rates are calculated.

questions.question: How do I calculate landed cost per unit?
questions.answer: Reconcile the total invoice and all applicable additional shipment acquisition charges once, then divide by the allocated quantity. For the base homogeneous shipment, $6,800 / 500 = $13.60 per unit.

questions.question: Is landed cost the same as the product invoice price?
questions.answer: Usually the cost boundary is broader: additional shipping, insurance, duties or clearance charges may apply. A bundled invoice can already include some or all of them. Add only charges that are not included.

questions.question: Are duties calculated as a percentage of the goods invoice?
questions.answer: The calculator does not choose a duty base or rate. It accepts a manually checked amount. Actual classification, origin, valuation and applicable trade rules need separate verification; the guide’s amounts are hypothetical.

questions.question: Should I include VAT or other import taxes?
questions.answer: Include an amount here only under the stated nonrecoverable-tax assumption. Recoverability is not determined by the tool. Cash paid at clearance can exceed economic cost if some tax is later recovered.

questions.question: Can I use this for several different products in one shipment?
questions.answer: The current tool evenly divides costs across homogeneous units. Mixed products may require value, weight, volume or product-specific allocation. It does not perform that allocation or choose an accounting policy.

questions.question: Does landed cost tell me my profit margin?
questions.answer: No. You also need the selling price and the full set of costs relevant to the margin definition. Advertising, fulfillment, marketplace fees and overhead are outside this acquisition worksheet; a price above landed cost can still produce a net loss.

limitations: Four hypothetical quotes use 500 identical units and manual USD amounts. They do not establish current transport prices, duty rates, tax recoverability or customs value.
This is an economic acquisition-cost worksheet, not an official inventory accounting policy, mixed-SKU allocation, legal interpretation of shipping terms or full net-profit calculation.
